screens.title: Understanding Unity's Physics Engine
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll build a clear mental model of Unity's physics: how a Rigidbody and a Collider work together, when to use triggers, and how forces produce believable motion. We'll start by defining the two core pieces of physics simulation: a Rigidbody gives an object mass and enables forces, while a Collider defines the object's physical shape. You will practice choosing collider types, learn why MeshColliders are expensive, and see how Physics Materials alter friction and bounciness to change game feel. We'll also walk through common pitfalls, like moving a physics object by changing its transform, and the correct use of FixedUpdate for physics calls. A concrete outcome: you'll be able to set up a player cube that jumps, pushes other objects with impulses, and detects pickups using triggers. That matters because predictable, performant physics directly affects gameplay: collisions that pass through, jitter, or slow frame rates break immersion. As you follow the lesson examples, notice the interplay of Rigidbody settings, collider choice, and ForceMode — these decisions determine control, stability, and performance. Consider how you would tune mass and friction for a slippery ice surface versus a rubber ball.

screens.title: What is a Rigidbody?
screens.narratorSegment: A Rigidbody is the component that tells Unity to treat a GameObject as part of the physics simulation. Concretely, it provides mass, allows gravity to act, and enables forces and torques to change velocity. Think of it as the object's physical identity: without a Rigidbody, a Collider only describes space but does not respond to forces or produce physics callbacks. A concrete example: a floating coin with only a BoxCollider will not generate collision events if neither it nor the player has a Rigidbody. Add a Rigidbody to the player or the coin and the physics engine will report contacts and allow AddForce to move them. A common misconception is that Rigidbody simply toggles gravity; in practice it replaces manual transform updates with a physics-driven motion pipeline. Misuse leads to problems: directly changing transform. position for a Rigidbody-controlled object can cause tunneling, jitter, or incorrect collision resolution. To move a Rigidbody, use AddForce, AddTorque, MovePosition, or MoveRotation so the engine integrates motion predictably. Key takeaway: attach a Rigidbody when you want mass, forces, collisions, and physics callbacks. How will you decide which objects need a Rigidbody in your scene?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Rigidbody
Rigidbody: the physics identity

When attached, a Rigidbody gives an object mass and makes it responsive to gravity, forces, and collisions. Colliders alone only declare shape.

Properties: mass, drag, angularDrag, useGravity, isKinematic.
Movement APIs: AddForce, AddTorque, MovePosition, MoveRotation.
Best practice: perform physics calls inside FixedUpdate for consistent results.
Key Takeaway

Attach a Rigidbody when you want authentic physics behaviour. Move via Rigidbody APIs to avoid unpredictable collisions.

Concrete example
Player cube with Rigidbody: mass 1, drag 0. When you call AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse) inside FixedUpdate, the Rigidbody gains upward velocity and the engine integrates gravity and collisions reliably.
Common mistake
Moving a Rigidbody by changing transform.position or rotation causes physics to be bypassed, producing tunnelling, jitter, or missed collision events.
Check your understanding
Name one scenario where you would prefer a kinematic Rigidbody instead of dynamic. Think about control and external forces.

screens.title: Static, Kinematic, and Dynamic Rigidbodies
screens.narratorSegment: Unity provides three practical Rigidbody modes you will select depending on whether an object should move under physics, be scripted, or remain fixed. A static object has no Rigidbody and is treated as immovable scenery. Use it for floors and walls where collisions should be resolved against the environment. A kinematic Rigidbody is controlled by code, not by physics forces; it does not respond to collisions by default but can push dynamic objects and is ideal for animated platforms. A dynamic Rigidbody is fully simulated: affected by gravity, forces, and collisions. An example: a moving platform animated via transform might be static or kinematic; prefer kinematic if it must interact with physics while being explicitly positioned. A common misconception is thinking kinematic equals non-colliding—kinematic objects still participate in collision resolution for other dynamic objects but do not have forces applied. Performance note: avoid giving non-moving scenery a Rigidbody; static colliders without a Rigidbody are cheaper. When designing a scene, ask whether the object should respond to forces or simply be a collision surface. Which objects in your level need to be dynamic, and which can be static or kinematic to balance control and performance?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Rigidbody Types
Mode comparison cards
Static (no Rigidbody)
Used for environment geometry. Cheapest for collisions. Does not move under physics.
Kinematic
Driven by code (MovePosition/MoveRotation). Can push dynamic bodies but ignores forces itself.
Dynamic
Fully simulated: affected by gravity, forces, and collision responses.
Key Takeaway

Pick the simplest mode that achieves your gameplay: static for scenery, kinematic for scripted motion, dynamic for physical interaction.

Concrete scenario
A moving platform that follows a path should be kinematic so it reliably moves along a curve and still pushes a dynamic player. Avoid making everyday static walls dynamic unless they must react to forces.
Misconception check
Some learners assume kinematic Rigidbodies are unaffected by collisions. In fact they collide, but they do not receive forces; they can push dynamics but remain under script control.
Question to reflect
Which mode would you choose for a destructible crate that should topple when hit, and why?

screens.title: Configuring Rigidbody Properties
screens.narratorSegment: Tuning Rigidbody properties is an iterative process that directly affects how objects accelerate, slow down, and rotate. Start with mass: it scales how forces change velocity. For example, a player with mass 1 responds quickly; an enemy armored vehicle with mass 50 will require larger forces to accelerate. Next set linear drag to control how quickly velocity decays during motion and angular drag to damp rotations. A high drag value simulates air resistance or sticky surfaces, while near-zero drag allows free sliding. Practical tuning steps: 1) Set mass to a realistic relative value across objects so forces behave proportionally. 2) Use AddForce with ForceMode. Acceleration for consistent acceleration that ignores mass differences, or Force for mass-sensitive pushes. 3) Play the scene and adjust drag to reach desired stopping distance. A typical mistake is setting mass very small and trying to compensate with tiny forces—this yields jitter and unpredictable collisions. Another is changing transform. position to move a Rigidbody; this bypasses the engine. Always test with collisions enabled and watch contact responses. As a takeaway, tune mass and drag together and validate behavior by applying a known force and observing displacement over time. What property would you change first to make a sliding object stop sooner?

keyIdea.text: Adjust mass, then drag values, and test with consistent force application. Use ForceMode to control mass sensitivity.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Configuring Rigidbody
Tuning steps
1
Set mass relatively
Choose mass values that reflect relative sizes; use larger forces for heavier objects.
2
Adjust drag
Increase drag to reduce sliding; angular drag to reduce unwanted spin.
3
Test with forces
Apply a known force and observe displacement; iterate on mass and drag until behavior matches design.
Key Takeaway

Mass and drag determine how objects respond to AddForce. Tune them together and test under realistic collisions.

Concrete example
If a player feels too floaty when jumping, increase mass or reduce jumpForce. If they slide too long on landing, raise drag slightly to shorten stopping distance.
Misconception
Reducing mass to make an object 'easier to push' then using the same forces often causes instability. Use ForceMode options or increase forces to match mass instead.
Try this
Apply a horizontal AddForce and measure how far an object travels. Adjust drag until travel distance matches your design constraint.

screens.title: Collider Types: Box, Sphere, Capsule, Mesh
screens.narratorSegment: Colliders declare the geometry Unity uses to detect overlaps and resolve collisions. Primitive colliders — Box, Sphere, Capsule — are fast and robust. A BoxCollider is perfect for crates and floors, SphereCollider for round objects like balls, and CapsuleCollider suits character bodies for smooth sliding. MeshCollider supports arbitrary shapes and higher fidelity; however, non-convex MeshColliders are expensive and problematic for moving objects. Use MeshCollider for static environment pieces or mark it convex for dynamic usage with caution. A common best practice is to approximate complex models with multiple primitive colliders to reduce computational cost while retaining acceptable collision fidelity. For example, a humanoid character might combine a CapsuleCollider for the torso and SphereColliders for hands and feet rather than relying on a detailed mesh. Misconceptions include assuming MeshColliders are always necessary for accuracy; in many gameplay scenarios primitives suffice. When profiling, check collision costs and replace expensive MeshColliders with primitive approximations where possible. Which collider combination would you use to approximate a car chassis while keeping runtime cost low? Collider Types: Box, Sphere, Capsule, Mesh means primitives are cheap and stable. meshcolliders give fidelity but cost performance; prefer convex or primitives for dynamic objects.. In practical terms, choosing shape fidelity versus performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Collider Types
Collider choices and guidance
BoxCollider
Best for rectangular objects and ground platforms.
SphereCollider
Ideal for balls and smooth collisions in any direction.
CapsuleCollider
Common for characters—smooth sliding and fewer snag points.
MeshCollider: use with caution
High-fidelity but expensive. Non-convex mesh colliders are unsuitable for dynamic objects. Prefer convex or primitive approximations for moving bodies.
Key Takeaway

Start with primitives. Use mesh colliders only when necessary and prefer convex for dynamic usage.

Concrete example
A character: one CapsuleCollider for the main body, SphereColliders for hands. A car: multiple BoxColliders for the chassis and SphereColliders for wheels approximation, instead of a full mesh collider.
Misconception
Believing mesh colliders always improve realism. Often approximations with primitives are visually indistinguishable in gameplay and far cheaper.

screens.title: How Rigidbodies and Colliders Interact
screens.narratorSegment: Unity's collision system combines Rigidbody motion and Collider shapes to compute contact, penetration resolution, and events. When a dynamic Rigidbody collides with another collider, the engine calculates contact points and resolves overlap by adjusting velocities and positions. The Collision object provided in OnCollisionEnter contains contact point data and the other collider's Rigidbody if present, allowing you to read where objects touched and apply reactions. Triggers are different: marking a Collider as 'Is Trigger' disables physical blocking and instead generates overlap events sent to OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit. A crucial rule: at least one of the interacting GameObjects must have a Rigidbody for either OnCollision or OnTrigger callbacks to be invoked. An example: a pickup set as trigger will only report OnTriggerEnter if the player or the pickup has a Rigidbody. Misconceptions include assuming trigger events supply collision contact points — triggers provide a Collider parameter without contact data. When you need impact location, use normal collisions and the Collision. contacts array. As a takeaway, choose collisions when you need physics response and contact details; choose triggers when you only need detection without physical interaction.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Interaction
Collision vs Trigger
Collisions block movement and produce contact details available through the Collision parameter. Triggers detect overlap without blocking and supply a Collider parameter.
Collision callbacks
OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, OnCollisionExit. Use Collision.contacts for impact points and normals.
Trigger callbacks
OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, OnTriggerExit. Use for pickups, zones, and detection without physical blocking.
Key Takeaway

Choose collision when you need physics response and contact data; choose trigger for non-blocking detection. Ensure at least one Rigidbody is present for callbacks.

Concrete example
A pickup marked Is Trigger: true inside a PickupZone will be detected by OnTriggerEnter if either the pickup or the player has a Rigidbody. If you need the exact hit location use a solid collider and OnCollisionEnter instead.
Misconception
Expecting trigger callbacks to include contact points. Triggers only provide the overlapping collider; no contact data is available.

screens.title: Collision and Trigger Callbacks in C#
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the essential C# callbacks for detecting collisions and triggers. OnCollisionEnter receives a Collision parameter containing contact points, the other collider, and the other Rigidbody if it exists. Use Collision. contacts to find where objects touched and reaction vectors to apply impulses. OnTriggerEnter receives a Collider parameter, which tells you which collider overlapped without contact details. Practically, when you set up a pickup item as a trigger, you typically implement OnTriggerEnter(Collider other) and then call CompareTag on other to confirm the player triggered the event before destroying or awarding the pickup. Remember: callbacks only fire if at least one object has a Rigidbody. Also ensure colliders start separated; overlapping colliders at scene start may not produce an Enter event until movement occurs. A common mistake is to expect both contact information and non-blocking behavior simultaneously; if you need contact data, use collision callbacks and allow physics to resolve contact. As you implement callbacks, log the names and use conditional logic to apply forces, update state, or destroy pickups. How will you structure your collision handlers to separate detection logic from game rules?

Collision handler sample
void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
{
    // collision.contacts contains contact points
    // collision.rigidbody references the other Rigidbody if present
    // Apply impulse to other object if it has a Rigidbody
}
Use Collision.contacts to get the impact normal and position. This is essential when you need to apply a reaction such as pushing another object away at the contact point.
Trigger handler sample
void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
{
    // other is the overlapping collider
    // Typical pattern: if (other.CompareTag("Player")) { Destroy(gameObject); }
}
Triggers are ideal for pickups and zones. They don't block motion and do not provide collision contact info.
Common Mistake

Expecting OnTriggerEnter to include impact points. Use collisions for contact data and triggers for detection only.

screens.title: Physics Materials: Friction and Bounciness
screens.narratorSegment: Physics Materials allow you to tune how surfaces interact by controlling friction and bounciness. Friction determines how readily two surfaces resist sliding relative to each other; high friction simulates rough surfaces like carpet, low friction simulates ice. Bounciness sets how much kinetic energy is returned after a collision, making balls bounce or dampening impact. PhysicMaterial assets are assigned to colliders so the engine computes combined behavior based on the interacting materials. An example: a rubber ball with high bounciness colliding with a low-bounce surface will bounce less than colliding with a similarly bouncy surface. Common pitfalls include expecting a material to work without considering collision relative velocities and masses — heavy objects with low elasticity may still appear to have little bounce. Also remember static friction versus dynamic friction: static friction affects when an object begins to slide, while dynamic friction affects motion during sliding. To tune feel, create a material, adjust friction and bounciness, and test interactions across the objects you expect to collide. What surface settings would you choose for a rolling bowling ball versus a rubber toy?

High bounciness

screens.title: Applying Forces and ForceMode
screens.narratorSegment: Applying forces is how you make Rigidbodies move under gameplay control. Rigidbody. AddForce accepts a Vector3 and a ForceMode that governs how the force affects velocity. The common modes are Force, Acceleration, Impulse, and VelocityChange. Force is the default for continuous acceleration that respects mass. Acceleration applies acceleration ignoring mass, useful for consistent control across differently weighted objects. Impulse applies an instantaneous change suitable for jumps or impacts. VelocityChange instantly changes velocity ignoring mass, giving you direct control but bypassing realistic mass effects. For example, to make a character jump use AddForce(Vector3. up * jumpForce, ForceMode. Impulse) inside FixedUpdate. For continuous movement like a jet push, AddForce(transform. forward * thrust, ForceMode. Force) provides steady acceleration. A common misconception is using Impulse for continuous forces; Impulse should be reserved for single, instantaneous events. Always call AddForce from FixedUpdate so the force integrates at the physics timestep. When testing, note how the same force produces different acceleration depending on mass unless you use Acceleration or VelocityChange. Which ForceMode will you use when you want identical acceleration for objects with different masses? Applying Forces and ForceMode means use force for mass-sensitive acceleration, acceleration to ignore mass, impulse for discrete impacts, and velocitychange for immediate velocity adjustments.. screens.title: FixedUpdate and the Physics Timestep
screens.narratorSegment: FixedUpdate runs at a consistent timestep synchronized to the physics engine, making it the correct place for applying forces, setting velocities, and moving Rigidbodies. Update runs once per rendered frame and varies with frame rate, which can cause physics to behave inconsistently on slower or faster machines. For example, applying AddForce in Update may produce different acceleration depending on frame rate, leading to jitter or inconsistent jump heights. FixedUpdate ensures physics integrations use uniform steps so collisions and impulses behave predictably. The practical process: read input in Update, store it in temporary variables, and apply forces in FixedUpdate. This separation prevents missed inputs and ensures deterministic physics calculations. A common mistake is reading input and immediately calling AddForce in Update; instead, capture input each frame and apply it in the next FixedUpdate. For deterministic gameplay, especially in networked or replay systems, sticking to FixedUpdate for physics logic reduces race conditions and jitter. How will you split input reading and physics application in your next controller script? content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › PlayerPhysicsController
Starter script pattern
// Pseudocode summary of the pattern
void Start() {
  rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
  if (rb == null) { enabled = false; }
}
void FixedUpdate() {
  // read cached input, apply movement via rb.AddForce(...)
  // on jump input: rb.AddForce(up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse)
}
void OnCollisionEnter(Collision c) { if (c.gameObject.CompareTag("Ground")) isGrounded = true; }
void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other) { if (other.CompareTag("Pickup")) Destroy(other.gameObject); }
This pattern reduces runtime errors, keeps physics deterministic, and cleanly separates detection from game logic. Test by toggling isKinematic on the other objects to observe different interactions.
Pro tip

Capture input in Update, then apply it in FixedUpdate. This avoids input being missed when FixedUpdate skips frames between updates.

screens.title: Pitfalls and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: This slide consolidates common mistakes to help you avoid time-consuming bugs. First, never move a physics object by setting transform. position or transform. rotation when that object has a Rigidbody; doing so bypasses integration and leads to tunnelling or jitter. Instead use Rigidbody. MovePosition, MoveRotation, AddForce, or AddTorque. Second, remember that OnCollision and OnTrigger callbacks require at least one Rigidbody on the interacting objects; missing Rigidbodies is a frequent cause of silent non-detection. Third, avoid non-convex MeshColliders on dynamic objects: they are computationally expensive and can produce unreliable collision behavior. Use primitive colliders to approximate shapes or mark the mesh convex for limited use. Fourth, be mindful of overlapping colliders at startup: if objects begin overlapped, Enter events may not fire; use Stay callbacks or ensure separation on scene start. Finally, always use FixedUpdate for physics operations. A useful checklist: replace transform-based movement, confirm Rigidbody presence, prefer primitives, review contact logs in OnCollisionEnter, and test behavior under varying frame rates. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll build a clear mental model of Unity's physics: how a Rigidbody and a Collider work together, when to use triggers, and how forces produce believable motion. We'll start by defining the two core pieces of physics simulation: a Rigidbody gives an object mass and enables forces, while a Collider defines the object's physical shape. You will practice choosing collider types, learn why MeshColliders are expensive, and see how Physics Materials alter friction and bounciness to change game feel. We'll also walk through common pitfalls, like moving a physics object by changing its transform, and the correct use of FixedUpdate for physics calls. A concrete outcome: you'll be able to set up a player cube that jumps, pushes other objects with impulses, and detects pickups using triggers. That matters because predictable, performant physics directly affects gameplay: collisions that pass through, jitter, or slow frame rates break immersion. As you follow the lesson examples, notice the interplay of Rigidbody settings, collider choice, and ForceMode — these decisions determine control, stability, and performance. Consider how you would tune mass and friction for a slippery ice surface versus a rubber ball.

These four objectives map directly to practical skills you will use when building physics-driven gameplay. First, you will distinguish static, kinematic, and dynamic Rigidbodies and choose the correct type for performance and control. I will show examples where a static object is part of the environment, a kinematic object is driven by code but not physics forces, and a dynamic object is fully simulated. Second, you'll configure Box, Sphere, Capsule, and Mesh colliders and understand the tradeoffs in fidelity and cost; the lesson demonstrates approximating complex shapes with multiple primitives. Third, you'll detect both collisions and triggers through C# callbacks, setting up OnCollision and OnTrigger handlers and ensuring at least one object has a Rigidbody so events fire. Fourth, you'll apply Physics Materials to control friction and bounciness, and use Rigidbody. AddForce with appropriate ForceMode values inside FixedUpdate. Each objective pairs a clear skill with why it matters in gameplay, so you can build stable, performant scenes and avoid common mistakes like moving Rigidbodies by changing transforms.

This second objectives slide focuses on the practical skills you'll implement and how to verify them. First, you will correctly attach and configure Rigidbody properties such as mass, drag, and angular drag. We'll examine how these values influence acceleration and stopping behavior, and you'll verify by observing a cube's response to AddForce. Second, you will set up primitive colliders and a convex MeshCollider when needed, learning to approximate complex geometry with multiple primitives to improve performance. Verification: inspect collision behavior and frame cost. Third, you'll write C# handlers for OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter, logging object names and using CompareTag to respond selectively. Test events by ensuring at least one object includes a Rigidbody. Fourth, you'll create and assign PhysicMaterial assets, adjusting dynamic and static friction and bounciness, and observe different outcomes when a ball hits surfaces. Each objective includes a short validation step you can run in the editor to confirm competency.

A Rigidbody is the component that tells Unity to treat a GameObject as part of the physics simulation. Concretely, it provides mass, allows gravity to act, and enables forces and torques to change velocity. Think of it as the object's physical identity: without a Rigidbody, a Collider only describes space but does not respond to forces or produce physics callbacks. A concrete example: a floating coin with only a BoxCollider will not generate collision events if neither it nor the player has a Rigidbody. Add a Rigidbody to the player or the coin and the physics engine will report contacts and allow AddForce to move them. A common misconception is that Rigidbody simply toggles gravity; in practice it replaces manual transform updates with a physics-driven motion pipeline. Misuse leads to problems: directly changing transform. position for a Rigidbody-controlled object can cause tunneling, jitter, or incorrect collision resolution. To move a Rigidbody, use AddForce, AddTorque, MovePosition, or MoveRotation so the engine integrates motion predictably. Key takeaway: attach a Rigidbody when you want mass, forces, collisions, and physics callbacks. How will you decide which objects need a Rigidbody in your scene?

Unity provides three practical Rigidbody modes you will select depending on whether an object should move under physics, be scripted, or remain fixed. A static object has no Rigidbody and is treated as immovable scenery. Use it for floors and walls where collisions should be resolved against the environment. A kinematic Rigidbody is controlled by code, not by physics forces; it does not respond to collisions by default but can push dynamic objects and is ideal for animated platforms. A dynamic Rigidbody is fully simulated: affected by gravity, forces, and collisions. An example: a moving platform animated via transform might be static or kinematic; prefer kinematic if it must interact with physics while being explicitly positioned. A common misconception is thinking kinematic equals non-colliding—kinematic objects still participate in collision resolution for other dynamic objects but do not have forces applied. Performance note: avoid giving non-moving scenery a Rigidbody; static colliders without a Rigidbody are cheaper. When designing a scene, ask whether the object should respond to forces or simply be a collision surface. Which objects in your level need to be dynamic, and which can be static or kinematic to balance control and performance?

Tuning Rigidbody properties is an iterative process that directly affects how objects accelerate, slow down, and rotate. Start with mass: it scales how forces change velocity. For example, a player with mass 1 responds quickly; an enemy armored vehicle with mass 50 will require larger forces to accelerate. Next set linear drag to control how quickly velocity decays during motion and angular drag to damp rotations. A high drag value simulates air resistance or sticky surfaces, while near-zero drag allows free sliding. Practical tuning steps: 1) Set mass to a realistic relative value across objects so forces behave proportionally. 2) Use AddForce with ForceMode. Acceleration for consistent acceleration that ignores mass differences, or Force for mass-sensitive pushes. 3) Play the scene and adjust drag to reach desired stopping distance. A typical mistake is setting mass very small and trying to compensate with tiny forces—this yields jitter and unpredictable collisions. Another is changing transform. position to move a Rigidbody; this bypasses the engine. Always test with collisions enabled and watch contact responses. As a takeaway, tune mass and drag together and validate behavior by applying a known force and observing displacement over time. What property would you change first to make a sliding object stop sooner?

Colliders declare the geometry Unity uses to detect overlaps and resolve collisions. Primitive colliders — Box, Sphere, Capsule — are fast and robust. A BoxCollider is perfect for crates and floors, SphereCollider for round objects like balls, and CapsuleCollider suits character bodies for smooth sliding. MeshCollider supports arbitrary shapes and higher fidelity; however, non-convex MeshColliders are expensive and problematic for moving objects. Use MeshCollider for static environment pieces or mark it convex for dynamic usage with caution. A common best practice is to approximate complex models with multiple primitive colliders to reduce computational cost while retaining acceptable collision fidelity. For example, a humanoid character might combine a CapsuleCollider for the torso and SphereColliders for hands and feet rather than relying on a detailed mesh. Misconceptions include assuming MeshColliders are always necessary for accuracy; in many gameplay scenarios primitives suffice. When profiling, check collision costs and replace expensive MeshColliders with primitive approximations where possible. Unity's collision system combines Rigidbody motion and Collider shapes to compute contact, penetration resolution, and events. When a dynamic Rigidbody collides with another collider, the engine calculates contact points and resolves overlap by adjusting velocities and positions. The Collision object provided in OnCollisionEnter contains contact point data and the other collider's Rigidbody if present, allowing you to read where objects touched and apply reactions. Triggers are different: marking a Collider as 'Is Trigger' disables physical blocking and instead generates overlap events sent to OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit. A crucial rule: at least one of the interacting GameObjects must have a Rigidbody for either OnCollision or OnTrigger callbacks to be invoked. An example: a pickup set as trigger will only report OnTriggerEnter if the player or the pickup has a Rigidbody. Misconceptions include assuming trigger events supply collision contact points — triggers provide a Collider parameter without contact data. When you need impact location, use normal collisions and the Collision. contacts array. As a takeaway, choose collisions when you need physics response and contact details; choose triggers when you only need detection without physical interaction.

Let's walk through the essential C# callbacks for detecting collisions and triggers. OnCollisionEnter receives a Collision parameter containing contact points, the other collider, and the other Rigidbody if it exists. Use Collision. contacts to find where objects touched and reaction vectors to apply impulses. OnTriggerEnter receives a Collider parameter, which tells you which collider overlapped without contact details. Practically, when you set up a pickup item as a trigger, you typically implement OnTriggerEnter(Collider other) and then call CompareTag on other to confirm the player triggered the event before destroying or awarding the pickup. Remember: callbacks only fire if at least one object has a Rigidbody. Also ensure colliders start separated; overlapping colliders at scene start may not produce an Enter event until movement occurs. A common mistake is to expect both contact information and non-blocking behavior simultaneously; if you need contact data, use collision callbacks and allow physics to resolve contact. Physics Materials allow you to tune how surfaces interact by controlling friction and bounciness. Friction determines how readily two surfaces resist sliding relative to each other; high friction simulates rough surfaces like carpet, low friction simulates ice. Bounciness sets how much kinetic energy is returned after a collision, making balls bounce or dampening impact. PhysicMaterial assets are assigned to colliders so the engine computes combined behavior based on the interacting materials. An example: a rubber ball with high bounciness colliding with a low-bounce surface will bounce less than colliding with a similarly bouncy surface. Common pitfalls include expecting a material to work without considering collision relative velocities and masses — heavy objects with low elasticity may still appear to have little bounce. Also remember static friction versus dynamic friction: static friction affects when an object begins to slide, while dynamic friction affects motion during sliding. To tune feel, create a material, adjust friction and bounciness, and test interactions across the objects you expect to collide. Applying forces is how you make Rigidbodies move under gameplay control. Rigidbody. AddForce accepts a Vector3 and a ForceMode that governs how the force affects velocity. The common modes are Force, Acceleration, Impulse, and VelocityChange. Force is the default for continuous acceleration that respects mass. Acceleration applies acceleration ignoring mass, useful for consistent control across differently weighted objects. Impulse applies an instantaneous change suitable for jumps or impacts. VelocityChange instantly changes velocity ignoring mass, giving you direct control but bypassing realistic mass effects. For example, to make a character jump use AddForce(Vector3. up * jumpForce, ForceMode. Impulse) inside FixedUpdate. For continuous movement like a jet push, AddForce(transform. forward * thrust, ForceMode. Force) provides steady acceleration. A common misconception is using Impulse for continuous forces; Impulse should be reserved for single, instantaneous events. Always call AddForce from FixedUpdate so the force integrates at the physics timestep. When testing, note how the same force produces different acceleration depending on mass unless you use Acceleration or VelocityChange. FixedUpdate runs at a consistent timestep synchronized to the physics engine, making it the correct place for applying forces, setting velocities, and moving Rigidbodies. Update runs once per rendered frame and varies with frame rate, which can cause physics to behave inconsistently on slower or faster machines. For example, applying AddForce in Update may produce different acceleration depending on frame rate, leading to jitter or inconsistent jump heights. FixedUpdate ensures physics integrations use uniform steps so collisions and impulses behave predictably. The practical process: read input in Update, store it in temporary variables, and apply forces in FixedUpdate. This separation prevents missed inputs and ensures deterministic physics calculations. A common mistake is reading input and immediately calling AddForce in Update; instead, capture input each frame and apply it in the next FixedUpdate. For deterministic gameplay, especially in networked or replay systems, sticking to FixedUpdate for physics logic reduces race conditions and jitter. This slide consolidates common mistakes to help you avoid time-consuming bugs. First, never move a physics object by setting transform. position or transform. rotation when that object has a Rigidbody; doing so bypasses integration and leads to tunnelling or jitter. Instead use Rigidbody. MovePosition, MoveRotation, AddForce, or AddTorque. Second, remember that OnCollision and OnTrigger callbacks require at least one Rigidbody on the interacting objects; missing Rigidbodies is a frequent cause of silent non-detection. Third, avoid non-convex MeshColliders on dynamic objects: they are computationally expensive and can produce unreliable collision behavior. Use primitive colliders to approximate shapes or mark the mesh convex for limited use. Fourth, be mindful of overlapping colliders at startup: if objects begin overlapped, Enter events may not fire; use Stay callbacks or ensure separation on scene start. Finally, always use FixedUpdate for physics operations. Collider: the geometric shape that defines where and how objects detect contact or overlap. Physics Material: an asset that controls friction and bounciness to influence sliding and rebound. These three concepts form the minimal vocabulary you'll use when designing interactions.
